extracted.intended_audience: trademark applicants and practitioners (attorneys and agents) handling ex parte appeals to the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules governing when and how to take an ex parte appeal from a trademark examining attorney to the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, including filing requirements, timing, evidence rules, remand, and review of final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness of Case for Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal may be taken to the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board from any final decision of the examining attorney, or from a second refusal on the same grounds or a repeated requirement; an application is ripe for appeal only when a final action has been issued (or the second/reflected repeated requirement has been issued).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second refusals or repeated requirements count as final only if all grounds/requirements are repeated. An Office action that repeats grounds but raises a new ground prevents finality. Cite: Trademark Act §20; 37 C.F.R. §§2.141, 2.64; TBMP §1201.01. Examples/case citations provided (e.g., In re Roberts, In re Page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Premature Final (when an Office action is improperly made final)
rubrics_metrics.description: A refusal or requirement should not be made final in a first action and should not be stated final until applicant has had at least one opportunity to reply to each ground or requirement; a final action should not issue until other matters (not to be the subject of the final action) are resolved and clear issues remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant believes finality was premature, raise it with the examining attorney (or managing/senior attorney) or file a petition under 37 C.F.R. §2.146. If an appeal was filed to preserve rights, advise the Board that final action was premature. The Board may decline to institute or vacate institution and forward the application back to the examiner; refund of appeal fee may be available if application reaches publication/registration on remand. See TBMP §1201.02 and notes with case citations and examples (amendments that raise new issues, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Premature Appeal (filing appeal before application is ripe)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal filed from a non-final action (e.g., a first refusal or where a new issue makes the action nonfinal) is premature; the Board has no jurisdiction to entertain a premature appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filed prematurely, the Board will notify applicant, forward the file to the examining attorney for appropriate action (often treated as an incomplete response), and may allow applicant to refile when/if a final action issues. Applicant may request refund of the fee if no later appeal is filed. See TBMP §1201.03 and cited cases (In re Page, In re Virshup).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance With Requirements Not Subject of Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: All formal requirements made by the examining attorney that are not the subject of the appeal must be complied with prior to filing an appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply with non-appealed requirements may result in the Board affirming the refusal to register for failure to comply, regardless of the Board’s disposition on appealed issues. See 37 C.F.R. §2.142(c) and TBMP §1201.04 (with case citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal versus Petition to the Director
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain matters must be addressed by petition to the Director rather than appeal, while substantive questions arising in ex parte prosecution are generally addressed by appeal to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations petitionable to the Director include: (1) repeated/formal requirements appropriate for petition under §2.63(b); (2) matters statutorily assigned to the Director; (3) invoking supervisory authority of the Director for procedural/nonfinal matters; (4) matters not provided for by Part 2; and (5) extraordinary situations requesting suspension/waiver of rules not required by statute. Substantive questions (e.g., issues under §§2–6 and 23 of the Act) are appropriate for appeal, not petition. A formal requirement that was the subject of a petition decided by the Director may not thereafter be appealed. See 37 C.F.R. §§2.63(b), 2.64(a), 2.146 and TBMP §1201.05 (with examples and citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing an Appeal — Notice and Fee Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal is taken by filing a written notice of appeal and paying the prescribed appeal fee; both notice and fee must be filed in the Office within six months of the final action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If notice or fee is not timely filed, the application will be deemed abandoned and the Board cannot entertain the appeal unless the application is revived by petition. The fee must be paid for each class appealed. See Trademark Act §20; 37 C.F.R. §§2.141, 2.142(a); TBMP §1202.01. Relevant citations and references to revival procedures are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal Fee Per Class and Multiple-class Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must pay an appeal fee for each class from which the appeal is taken; in multiple-class applications the applicant must specify which classes are being appealed if fees do not cover all classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fee is insufficient or classes not specified, Board will issue notice to pay additional fees or specify classes; if applicant fails to do so within time limit, Board will apply fees to classes in ascending order beginning with lowest-numbered class. If final refusal pertains to some but not all classes, applicant may either appeal whole application (paying only for classes appealed) or request to divide the application to sever classes with no final refusal. Failure to appeal a class with a final refusal will result in abandonment of that class unless there is a timely request for reconsideration that later results in non-final action. See TBMP §1202.01 and §1202.05 with case citations (In re MGA Entertainment, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time for Filing an Appeal (six‑month deadline)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal to the Board must be filed within six months from the date of the final action being appealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If notice is timely filed but fee is not, appeal is untimely and application will be abandoned. Filing of a request for reconsideration does not extend or stay the six‑month appeal period — to preserve appeal rights, applicant should file a notice of appeal within six months even if reconsideration is pending. Methods for filing (facsimile for notice; ESTTA encouraged) and use of certificates of mailing/transmission are discussed. See 37 C.F.R. §2.142(a); TBMP §1202.02 and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Appeal — Permitted Filing Methods and Special Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of appeal may be filed by facsimile transmission as well as by ordinary filing methods including electronic filing through ESTTA; facsimile filing is permitted only for the notice of appeal (not for other papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ESTTA electronic filing is strongly encouraged; certificate of mailing/transmission and Express Mail procedures are available. If filing by facsimile, follow the limited facsimile rules. See 37 C.F.R. §§2.126, 2.195, 2.197–2.198 and TBMP §1202.02 with procedural tips (ESTTA timing, update delays, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Request for Reconsideration of Final Office Action
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for reconsideration filed between issuance of a final action and expiration of the appeal period does not extend the time to file a notice of appeal; the examiner normally will reply within the six‑month period if the request is filed within three months of the final action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments accompanying requests for reconsideration after final action will be entered if they comply with rules; if applicant fails to file notice of appeal within six months and reconsideration fails and no new final action is issued, the application may be deemed abandoned. See 37 C.F.R. §2.64(b) and TBMP §1201.01 and §1202.02 (notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal Briefs — Form and Content Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal briefs must comply with applicable form requirements set out by the Board and rules governing content, length, and argumentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1203 (Form of Brief) sets out formatting, required sections, and other formalities. (The chapter includes subparts on timing for filing briefs, what materials may be submitted with briefs, cases that may be cited, and waiver of claims or requirements in a brief.) The examining attorney may not raise new grounds of refusal in an appeal brief. See TBMP §1203.01–.02 and related notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and Sequence for Filing Briefs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a specified timeline: applicant's main brief is filed first, followed by the examining attorney's brief, then applicant's reply brief; rules allow for extensions of time under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsections TBMP §1203.02(a)–(d) detail timeframes for each brief, extension procedures, what material may be introduced with briefs (and limitations), and cases that may be cited. If a ground was not timely raised in prosecution, it generally will not be considered. See TBMP §1203.02 and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of Claim or Requirement in Brief
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may waive a claim or requirement in a brief, thereby removing it from the issues on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1203.02(g) addresses waiver in briefs — when applicant expressly abandons a claim or requirement in its brief, the Board will not consider it. Properly indicating waiver can affect scope of appeal and possible remand consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of Evidence During Appeal — General Rule (untimely evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence submitted after the filing of an appeal is generally untimely and will not be considered by the Board except under limited circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1207.01 explains exceptions: evidence may be considered if submitted with a timely request for reconsideration, if considered due to actions of a non‑offering party, upon remand for new refusal, or if the Board remands for additional evidence. Requests to remand to take additional evidence are addressed in TBMP §1207.02 and related subsections. Letters of protest and other evidentiary submissions have special treatment rules. See TBMP §1207 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request to Remand for Additional Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may request the Board to remand the application to the examining attorney for consideration of additional evidence; the Board may remand on its own initiative or upon request by the examining attorney or applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1209 and §1207.02 explain remand grounds and procedures. Evidence filed with a timely request for reconsideration or upon remand for a new refusal may be considered; remand may be for the purpose of allowing submission/evaluation of evidence that could affect registrability. See relevant notes and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Internet, Database, and Third‑Party Material as Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has rules for evaluating online materials, database evidence (e.g., Nexis), third‑party registrations, judicial notice, and an applicant's own materials when offered as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1208.01–.05 discuss reliability, authentication, printouts, dates of capture, probative weight, and when judicial notice may be taken. Third‑party registrations and Internet evidence often require foundation or may be subject to limited evidentiary value. Applicant's own materials also have specific treatment. See TBMP §1208 and cited cases for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of Application During Appeal — General Limitations and Requests to Divide
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to an application after filing an appeal are restricted; a request to divide (sever) classes or goods/services may be filed in certain ways depending on whether the notice of appeal was submitted electronically or on paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1205.01 and §1205.02 explain when amendments are allowed and procedures for requests to divide: §1205.02(a) for notices submitted electronically and §1205.02(b) for paper filings. If goods/services or classes are divided out, those divided portions may proceed to publication/registration while appeal is instituted for the remaining classes. See TBMP §1202.01 and §1205 for detailed procedure and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment to Allege Use; Statement of Use During Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures and restrictions govern amendments to allege use and statements of use in intent-to-use applications during the appeal process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1206.01–.02 detail when amendments to allege use and statements of use may be submitted and how examining attorney review of specimen/use issues may produce new refusals that are separate from the appealed issues (and may be pursued after Board decision). See TBMP §1217 note regarding examining attorney's later actions on statements of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand — Grounds and Parties Who May Seek It
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may remand an application to the examining attorney upon the Board’s own initiative, upon request by the examining attorney, upon a granted letter of protest, or upon request by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1209.01–.04 explain these bases for remand. Remand may be used to allow additional examination or to consider submissions not previously part of the record. See TBMP §1209 and linked notes and cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval for Publication During Appeal and Appeal Fee Refunds
rubrics_metrics.description: If, upon remand, the examining attorney determines the application is in condition for publication (or for registration on the Supplemental Register), the applicant may request refund of the previously submitted appeal fee; if a new final action issues and applicant wishes to appeal, the previously paid fee may be applied to the new appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1201.02 and §1209 (and notes) explain Board letters and procedures informing applicant of remand results and refund/apply‑fee options. See examples and case citations in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment During Appeal and Consequences for Unappealed Classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file a notice of appeal and/or pay required appeal fees will cause abandonment; in multiple-class applications, classes not appealed or for which requirements are not complied with may be deemed abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1202.01–.02 and notes explain abandonment rules, effect of partial fees, and that certain timely responses (e.g., request for reconsideration without notice of appeal) may be treated as incomplete responses leading to abandonment and making petitions to revive subject to limitations. Case law and procedural citations included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation or Assignment of Cited Registration Affecting Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Cancellation or assignment of a cited registration during appeal may affect the appeal outcome and the Board's treatment of cited registrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1212 addresses how cancellation or assignment of a cited registration is to be treated; relevant procedural consequences and examples are given (see TBMP §1212 and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension, Consolidation, and Alternative Positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may suspend an appeal (e.g., pending related proceedings), consolidate related appeals, and permit parties to present alternative positions in briefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §§1213–1215 cover suspension and consolidation authority and strategic/ procedural rules for presenting alternative arguments or fall-back positions. Guidance includes when suspension or consolidation is appropriate and how alternative positions should be presented in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral Hearing Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may request and the Board may hold oral hearings in ex parte appeals subject to Board rules governing scheduling, format, and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1216 contains rules on requesting an oral hearing, scheduling, what to expect at hearing, and related procedural matters. The Board may limit scope and will follow briefing and evidence rules established in the appeal record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Decision — Scope, Rationale, and Limitations on Remand
rubrics_metrics.description: In its final decision the Board will determine whether the examining attorney's decision was correct; the Board may affirm on any rationale supported by the record and need not accept examiner’s rationale; the Board normally will consider all issues on appeal and may render class‑specific outcomes, but cannot remand the case in its final decision except in limited circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining attorney may not raise new grounds during appeal (except upon remand), but may advance new arguments/citations supporting earlier-raised grounds. The Board may affirm one issue and decline to reach others in certain circumstances. The Board generally lacks authority to remand in its final decision in an ex parte appeal (37 C.F.R. §2.142), though it may suspend and remand if an issue not previously raised appears to render the mark unregistrable; it may also recommend voluntary applicant corrections for minor defects if applicant prevails on other issues. Case law examples and caveats are given (see TBMP §1217 and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reopening After Final Decision (Amendment, Disclaimer, Director Orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application decided on appeal will not be reopened except for entry of a disclaimer under §6 or upon order of the Director; a petition to the Director to reopen is considered only upon sufficient cause for consideration of new matters not adjudicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1218 explains when the Board or Director may reopen an application after final decision (disclaimer entry, Director-ordered reopening for sufficient cause), and notes that appellate courts may remand to the Office for further examination and additional evidence. See 37 C.F.R. §2.142(g) and cases cited (e.g., remand after Federal Circuit decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of Final Decision — Request for Reconsideration (timing and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for rehearing, reconsideration, or modification of the Board’s final decision in an ex parte appeal must be filed within one month from the date of the decision (subject to extension for sufficient cause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If timely filed, the time for filing an appeal or commencing civil review runs for two months after action on the request. The examining attorney may also request reconsideration within one month. See 37 C.F.R. §2.144 and TBMP §1219.01 (with citations and examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of Final Decision — Appeal to Federal Circuit or Civil Action
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant dissatisfied with the Board's final decision may seek review by appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit or by filing a civil action for review of the Board’s decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TBMP §1219.02 provides procedure references (TBMP §§901–903) and notes that the Court may remand the application to the Office during pendency of the appeal for further examination and submission of additional evidence. See Trademark Act §21 and 37 C.F.R. §2.145.
